title: How ISVs are unlocking European workloads using Google Cloud Dedicated technology
raw_text: Across Europe, organizations handling sensitive workloads in regulated sectors — such as financial services, healthcare, critical infrastructure, and the public sector — are trying to modernize their infrastructure while adhering to strict local data governance standards, including SecNumCloud in France and BSI C3A in Germany. To help organizations accomplish this, Google Cloud Dedicated provides the architectural, security, and API consistency of Google Cloud in locally governed environments managed by independent domestic operators. But infrastructure is only the starting point. Organizations also need to transform the software ecosystem they rely on every day. To meet regional sovereignty requirements, organizations acquire and run these software solutions through trusted local entities — such as S3NS in France (a joint venture majority-owned and managed by Thales) and a newly formed German entity that will also be owned and managed by Thales, currently in preview. These local entities operate dedicated infrastructure stacks, help maintain operational custody, and handle customer data within independent jurisdictional boundaries. Today, we are highlighting the expanding independent software vendor (ISV) ecosystem validated on Google Cloud Dedicated, enabling French and German organizations to run their critical enterprise software in environments designed to support their sovereign and regulatory needs. The local partner model: Cloud capability under domestic custody Deploying in a sovereign boundary should not require an organization to sacrifice software choice or rewrite its enterprise applications.Because Google Cloud Dedicated provides architectural and API consistency with Google Cloud, validated enterprise software runs directly inside these partner-operated environments without custom re-platforming. This model provides European enterprises with three concrete advantages: Localized operational custody : Infrastructure operations, software quarantine procedures, and day-to-day administrative access are under the direct management of local European partners operating with specialized remote technical escalations governed by strict, partner-supervised escorted access controls. Broad software choice : Regulated institutions can deploy industry-standard tools for identity governance, cyber resilience, simulation, and data streaming natively in their sovereign perimeter. Streamlined compliance : Organizations fulfill national frameworks like SecNumCloud and BSI guidelines while preserving familiar CI/CD pipelines, APIs, and developer workflows. Software choice is the true bottleneck for sovereign migrations When highly regulated European institutions consider moving to a sovereign cloud, the infrastructure itself is rarely the primary roadblock. The real bottleneck is software.Historically, pursuing strict sovereignty meant accepting compromises: Rewriting applications from scratch or maintaining custom, brittle tooling because mainstream enterprise platforms were unavailable. Forcing security, engineering, and data teams to abandon the industry-standard tools they use daily in favor of untested niche alternatives. Sidelining high-impact initiatives like real-time fraud scoring, automated DevSecOps, and modern identity governance simply because the required ISVs could not legally or technically operate in the environment. Because Google Cloud Dedicated maintains architectural and API consistency with Google Cloud, leading global and European software providers can deploy their proven platforms directly inside national, domestic operator-managed boundaries. Regulated organizations retain the software, automated pipelines, and operational standards they rely on — without sacrificing compliance or operational custody. Validated ISVs on Google Cloud Dedicated Deploying enterprise software on Google Cloud Dedicated and S3NS isn't just about hosting an application locally; it’s about pairing proven software engines with sovereign operations. Here is how these joint architectures unlock strategic value for European enterprises: Cohesity on Google Cloud Dedicated (Sovereign cyber resilience): Cohesity has many options to meet organizational data sovereignty objectives, whether on-premises or in the cloud with Google Cloud Dedicated. This is done through a unified, cyber resilient, AI-powered data platform — Cohesity Data Cloud — that is sovereign-by-design, making it easier to protect, manage, recover, and have visibility into data, while supporting compliance with data sovereignty requirements. For example, running Cohesity directly in the S3NS perimeter combines Cohesity’s Zero Trust cyber resilience architecture designed for immutability with local operational custody. Customers gain advanced threat hunting, cyber vaulting, and recovery orchestration that powers quick, clean, and trusted cyber-recovery from ransomware threats without allowing diagnostic telemetry, secondary backup copies, or operational keys to traverse external networks. GitLab on Google Cloud Dedicated (Secure, compliant software delivery pipelines): Combining GitLab’s DevSecOps platform with Google Cloud Dedicated allows defense, aerospace, and public sector engineering teams to ship code at commercial velocity. Proprietary source code, vulnerability scans, and CI/CD artifact registries stay contained behind the partner-operated boundary, significantly reducing audit friction of using public SaaS code repositories. Ansys, part of Synopsys, on Google Cloud Dedicated (High-performance sovereign engineering simulation): Pairing Ansys, part of Synopsys, high-performance computing simulation workflows with the dedicated compute clusters of Google Cloud Dedicated gives European manufacturers the massive scale needed for aerodynamic, fluid, and structural modeling. Highly sensitive intellectual property, blueprints, and digital twins designed to keep intellectual property within regional boundaries and national jurisdiction while running at cloud speed. Memority on Google Cloud Dedicated / S3NS (Audit-ready sovereign identity governance): Integrating Memority’s identity factory platform directly into the S3NS SecNumCloud-qualified environment provides regulated entities with capabilities designed to support their NIS2 and DORA compliance requirements with the PREMI3NS SecNumCloud-qualified environment. Organizations can manage and audit millions of identities without building custom IAM infrastructure or exposing access tokens to non-European cloud services. "Our customers — from critical infrastructure operators to financial institutions — share the same requirement: an enterprise-grade IAM platform capable of managing millions of identities while meeting the highest standards of digital sovereignty. As NIS2 and DORA reshape the regulatory landscape, this requirement has become a business-critical imperative. S3NS enables us to address it at scale by providing a comprehensive IAM platform hosted in a SecNumCloud-qualified cloud environment, with built-in capabilities supporting the auditability, traceability, and operational resilience expected under these regulations,” said Francis Grégoire, Deputy CEO, Memority. RackWare on Google Cloud Dedicated (De-risked cloud migration): Running RackWare’s automated migration and disaster recovery engines on Google Cloud Dedicated gives organizations a low-friction bridge from on-premises data centers into sovereign cloud environments. Teams can replicate, synchronize, and failover complex enterprise operating environments, bypassing the prohibitive cost and timeline of manual application refactoring. Striim on Google Cloud Dedicated (Real-time data streaming without jurisdictional risk): Combining Striim’s continuous change data capture engine with the local boundaries of Google Cloud Dedicated enables organizations to feed live operational analytics and fraud models without batch delays. Financial institutions and logistics leaders can stream sensitive customer and payment transactions in sub-second intervals, with strong technical assurances that streaming pipelines remain bound to local infrastructure. "Regulated organizations should not have to choose between modern, real-time data and the control their environments demand. By making Striim available on Google Cloud Dedicated, we can help customers securely move and continuously deliver trusted data to the systems that power critical operations, analytics, and AI without ever compromising on sovereignty or resilience,” said Phillip Cockrell, SVP of Business Development, Striim. UPS Capital integrated Striim’s real-time streaming technology with analytics models to power its DeliveryDefense address verification and delivery security system. By streaming and validating transaction and delivery data continuously without batch lag, UPS assesses risk scoring in real time — a capability European logistics and financial operators can now deploy directly in their sovereign boundary. Red Hat on Google Cloud Dedicated (Operational consistency on open hybrid platforms): Deploying Red Hat Enterprise Linux and OpenShift across Google Cloud Dedicated bridges on-premises infrastructure and sovereign cloud environments. Engineering teams maintain their existing operating runtimes, container standards, and administrative toolsets across sites, avoiding vendor lock-in and eliminating the operational retraining typically required when moving to sovereign stacks. Saviynt on Google Cloud Dedicated (Zero-trust access governance across sovereign assets): Deploying Saviynt’s privileged access management and identity governance inside the sovereign boundary allows enterprises to centrally enforce least-privilege security across critical databases and workloads. Security administrators maintain automated role lifecycles and complete audit logs without exposing access intelligence to offshore management planes. Tsuga on Google Cloud Dedicated (Telemetry and observability): Tsuga’s bring-your-own-cloud (BYOC) observability platform deployed inside a customer's dedicated VPC resolves one of the biggest security exposures in regulated IT: transmitting production telemetry to third-party SaaS monitoring providers. By processing all traces, metrics, and logs on local storage, organizations achieve full observability, reduce external data egress costs, and help protect sensitive operational data. MongoDB on Google Cloud Dedicated (Modern data velocity with domestic residency): Running MongoDB Enterprise Advanced on Google Cloud Dedicated gives developers the flexibility of the document model while adhering to strict regional isolation requirements. Regulated organizations can rapidly build modern, real-time applications and customer portals using modern development patterns without being forced onto legacy relational database architectures. Ispirer on Google Cloud Dedicated (Automated legacy modernization): Pairing Ispirer’s automated database conversion toolkit with Google Cloud Dedicated addresses a key friction point in database modernization: the complexity of migrating legacy database engines. Automated code and schema conversion shrinks complex multi-year migration timelines into predictable, low-risk deployments on modern sovereign infrastructure. "Every migration is really a risk decision. Offering the Ispirer toolkit on Google Cloud Dedicated gives customers over 27 years of deterministic conversion experience—that's the value we consistently hear back from client teams,” said Natallia Bespalova, CEO, Ispirer Systems. Splunk integration with Google Cloud Dedicated (sovereign log collection, observability, and SIEM integration): Splunk now supports Google Cloud Dedicated as a first-class log source. Extensions to the open-source OpenTelemetry Collector allow organizations to export logs from Google Cloud Dedicated environments into Splunk Enterprise using the Google Cloud Pub/Sub receiver and the Splunk HTTP Event Collector (HEC) exporter, alongside enhancements to the Splunk Add-on for Google Cloud for direct log collection Additionally, Splunk Observability Cloud now supports Google Cloud Dedicated through its Infrastructure Monitoring cloud integration, which connects projects to pull metrics and metadata from services so teams can monitor resource and application health. title: Alibaba touts 62% lower task costs with Qwen4-Max, adds cyber safeguards
raw_text: Alibaba has released Qwen4-Max, a 2.4-trillion-parameter flagship model, claiming it reduces the average cost of completing professional tasks by 62% compared with its predecessor while introducing additional safeguards against offensive cybersecurity capabilities and other high-risk uses. “According to Work360 — a proprietary benchmark evaluating performance on challenging industry tasks across 721 specialized fields — Qwen4-Max outperforms its predecessor, Qwen3.8-Max, overall while using 35% fewer tokens at High effort reasoning mode and reducing the average cost per task by around 60%,” Alibaba said in a blog post. The Qwen team’s announcement puts the average task cost at $1.67 for Qwen4-Max, compared with $4.43 for Qwen3.8-Max, representing a 62% reduction. The model keeps the 2.4-trillion-parameter mixture-of-experts backbone of its predecessor, Qwen3.8-Max, but activates about 71 billion parameters per token instead of about 95 billion, the company said. It supports a 1-million-token context window. The company attributed the savings to lower token use and new list prices of $1.50 per million input tokens and $4.50 per million output tokens, down from $2 and $6. Anthropic lists Claude Opus 5.5 at $20 per million output tokens. Sanchit Vir Gogia, chief analyst at Greyhound Research, said enterprises should treat the figure as a vendor benchmark rather than an assured reduction in their own AI spending. The relevant measure, he said, is the cost of an accepted result, including retries, reasoning tokens, and employee time spent checking outputs. “Alibaba has published the mileage it got on its own road, and a buyer’s bill depends on the road the buyer drives,” Gogia said. Yash Kadakia, founder and CTO of Security Brigade, said enterprises should measure successful task completion rather than token prices alone. “An enterprise should benchmark what it costs to complete 1,000 real business tasks successfully, not what it costs to generate a million tokens,” Kadakia said. Alibaba also cited improvements across coding and agentic evaluations, including Code Arena and Agents’ Last Exam. In an automotive manufacturing demonstration, the company said Qwen4-Max reduced manual workpiece programming time from approximately 475 minutes to 24 minutes. Security claims need independent testing Alongside the cost figures, Alibaba set out changes to what the model learns about hacking at the training-data stage. “For cybersecurity, we filter data according to the specific purpose of each task, retaining data for defensive tasks such as vulnerability verification, detection, and remediation, while removing data for offensive tasks aimed at enhancing attack capabilities,” the Alibaba blog post said. The company said code security checks added during training lifted the share of functions passing both functionality and security tests on Last Secure Code Bench from 22% to 31.8%. Its internal security experts found the model’s defensive capabilities had “improved substantially,” the post added. Kadakia questioned whether offensive and defensive cybersecurity knowledge can be reliably separated through training-data filtering. “One of the fundamental challenges with cybersecurity AI is that offensive and defensive knowledge are largely the same knowledge,” he said, noting that understanding SQL injection is necessary both to exploit and prevent it. Gogia said the distinction requires independent validation, recommending that CISOs seek assessments from government evaluators or established external red teams rather than rely solely on Alibaba’s internal testing. The announcement follows an October investigation by Canadian AI company Cohere, which reported that an earlier Alibaba model, Qwen3.8-Flash-Next, attempted to send a test file to an Alibaba Cloud storage destination in Beijing during a security test. Cohere said its sandbox blocked the request. A subsequent investigation by Check Point replayed the behaviour 64 times and found 52 different destination hosts. It suggested unpredictable model behaviour was a more likely explanation than a deliberately configured backdoor. The incident involved an experimental model, not Qwen4-Max. Besides, Government evaluators have begun testing Chinese models independently. In July, the US Center for AI Standards and Innovation found that the safeguards on Z.ai’s GLM-5.2 allowed assistance with agentic cyber exploit development. Gogia said CISOs should treat Alibaba’s filter “as a promise until a government evaluator or an established outside red team has tested it.” Data governance and open-weight risks For enterprises outside China, Gogia said the geographic scope of Alibaba’s global service, prompt-retention policies, and jurisdiction governing stored data should be considered before deploying the model for sensitive workloads. He pointed to prompt retention of up to 30 days and longer retention of flagged content, including under zero-retention arrangements. Kadakia said enterprises should examine where prompts, retrieved documents, tool outputs, and logs are processed, who can access them, and what permissions agents have across internal systems. “The biggest risk with enterprise AI is no longer simply what information employees type into a chatbot. It is what an autonomous agent can access, what decisions it can make, and what actions it can execute across connected enterprise systems,” he said. Alibaba also plans to release smaller Qwen4 models with open weights. Kadakia said developers modifying those models through fine-tuning should not assume the original security safeguards will remain intact. “Safety training is not a permanent property of a model,” he said, recommending fresh adversarial testing and controls over tool access for customised versions. Gogia similarly recommended reassessing each modified model rather than automatically inheriting the original model’s security assurances. The article originally appeared on InfoWorld .

title: The benign true positive: When trusted AI agents look like attackers
raw_text: A coding agent opens hundreds of files, launches command-line tools and connects to an internal service to complete a task. A support agent authenticates to several systems, retrieves customer records and updates another application. A workflow agent enumerates cloud resources in seconds, then moves to the next stage of its assignment. To an endpoint, identity, or cloud security platform, these sequences can resemble reconnaissance, credential access, lateral movement, or the early stages of exfiltration. The control is accurately identifying behavior associated with an attack, and the agent is carrying out an approved business task. I am beginning to see this pattern as enterprises deploy AI agents across software development, customer support, finance, IT and security. I call it the benign true positive: an accurate detection of attack-like behavior generated by legitimate machine activity. For CISOs, this exposes a foundational assumption beneath behavioral security . For decades, attack-like behavior justified immediate suspicion because legitimate systems rarely operated with the speed, breadth and autonomy now common among AI agents. That assumption is weakening, and security leaders need to prepare their teams, processes and technology portfolios for the consequences. Behavioral baselines were built around people Modern detection systems rely heavily on patterns associated with expected human activity. People read files at a human pace, move between applications in recognizable sequences, and generally interact with systems one action at a time. An account that suddenly enumerates thousands of resources or launches a chain of processes across several environments deserves investigation. AI agents follow a different operating pattern. They gather context broadly, perform tasks in parallel and move across systems according to the needs of an assigned objective. A coding agent may inspect an entire repository before changing a few lines. A support agent may authenticate to several applications because resolving a customer request requires data from each one. The resulting telemetry frequently matches the signals security tools were designed to detect. Existing controls will keep generating alerts, and those alerts will often be technically correct. Security teams must determine whether the behavior reflects an authorized task, a compromised agent, manipulated instructions, stolen credentials, or an attacker imitating normal agent activity. A broad suppression rule may reduce noise but also create a blind spot. Attackers will naturally look for trusted agent identities, approved workflows and familiar machine-speed patterns that help them blend into the environment. Intent becomes the missing layer Security tools observe actions such as process launches, file reads, authentication events, API calls, or network connections. Intent sits in the surrounding context. Investigators need to know who owns the agent, what task it was assigned, who initiated the task, which systems it was authorized to use, what data it could access and whether its actions stayed within approved boundaries. They also need to determine whether another user, process, or external input altered the agent’s instructions. Those answers may be distributed across identity systems, agent orchestration platforms, cloud infrastructure, business applications, ticketing systems and the security stack. Reconstructing the event requires correlation across these sources and a clear account of what the agent was trying to accomplish. A large enterprise may soon operate thousands of agents across business and technical functions. Human analysts cannot manually reconstruct every event at that scale. Security operations will need investigative capacity that can recover intent at machine speed and present conclusions grounded in observable evidence. 3 investment priorities for CISOs 1. Agent identity and governance The first priority is agent identity and governance . Every agent should have a clear owner, a defined purpose, credentials scoped to its responsibilities and documented access to applications, tools and data. The SOC should be able to connect each action to the workflow, user request, or business process that initiated it. This requires an inventory of active agents, lifecycle controls, access reviews, approval requirements for sensitive actions and audit trails that connect behavior to an accountable owner. Shared service accounts and broad permissions slow investigations and make containment harder. Purpose-specific identities and task provenance give the SOC the context needed to identify misuse. 2. Investigation architecture The second priority is investigation architecture. Security leaders should evaluate whether their current stack can assemble evidence across endpoint, identity, cloud, network, SaaS and agent platforms. A useful system should reconstruct the sequence of events, apply organizational context, document missing information and explain how it reached a conclusion. AI investments in the SOC should support evidence gathering, cross-system correlation, adaptive reasoning and clear escalation whenever the available data cannot support a confident determination. 3. Team design The third priority is team design. Analysts will increasingly govern systems that investigate both human and machine behavior. Their expertise will shape operating boundaries, exception handling, detection logic and the context used during investigations. Security leaders should invest in detection engineering, threat hunting, identity governance and agent oversight skills. Analysts need time and authority to examine recurring behavioral collisions, refine access policies, improve workflows and challenge automated conclusions. Each benign true positive can become a source of operational learning about how agents are being used and where controls need to mature. A new operating model for the SOC The traditional SOC sends alerts to analysts, who gather evidence and decide what happened. AI agents will add another source of high-volume activity, and many resulting alerts will be accurate detections of legitimate behavior. The SOC needs an operating model built around rapid interpretation. For an authorized event, the investigation should show that a specific agent accessed particular systems under an approved identity, pursued a valid task, remained within its permissions and produced no evidence of deviation. For a risky event, it should show where the activity exceeded the agent’s expected scope and why human review or containment is required. This level of clarity preserves sensitive detections, keeps analysts focused on cases that demand judgment, and creates a practical path for building trust in increasingly autonomous systems through visible evidence, explicit accountability and measurable outcomes. Preparing for the next source of alert volume CISOs should begin by mapping where agents already operate across the organization. Many will discover activity introduced through developer tools, SaaS platforms, departmental automation and enterprise applications with embedded agent capabilities. The next step is to connect agent ownership, identity, permissions, task provenance and policy to security operations. Teams should test how existing controls respond to representative agent workflows and track benign true positives as a distinct operational category. AI agents are changing the meaning of normal behavior. Security leaders who prepare now can preserve visibility, strengthen governance and build a SOC capable of understanding the purpose behind machine-speed activity. Trusted machines will increasingly look like attackers. The organizations that can recover intent quickly will be best positioned to tell the difference.

title: AI-written patches are becoming attack maps for hackers
raw_text: This summer, the maintainers of vm2, an open-source JavaScript sandboxing library with 1 million downloads per week, shipped fixes for 34 separate sandbox-escape vulnerabilities and Anthropic’s Claude co-wrote 19 of them. Weeks later, a security researcher pointed an AI agent at one of the advisories and asked for a way around the patch. The agent delivered. Shayaun Nejad, lead product security engineer at Rubrik, ran vulnerability variant analysis on the vm2 patch while preparing for a talk he held at the recent [un]prompted AI security conference in San Francisco. He wanted to highlight the challenges his development team faced when dealing with a flood of AI-discovered vulnerabilities, and noted that the same bugs kept being rediscovered later in new testing runs despite being fixed by AI-assisted pipelines. “Sometimes the [vulnerability] variant wouldn’t be caught until the model variation got better or the model used chaining analysis at a higher degree once it improved in order to find those variants,” he said. “Sometimes it was in the exact same spot, sometimes it was something that was related, that was a neighbor, but variant analysis is basically something that has been popping up, and it’s a context magnet, too.” With the rate of published CVEs higher than ever due to AI assistance, software developers are actually disclosing the types of vulnerabilities their platforms are susceptible to, and the patches for these flaws can serve as blueprints for attackers, Nejad warned. Sometimes it’s as simple as pointing an AI agent at a codebase with its historical vulnerabilities as context and telling it to go hunt for variants, he said. Rubrik’s experience reflects a broader asymmetry that other researchers have observed in recent months: AI models have become very good at offense — finding vulnerabilities and building exploits — while their defensive skills, such as writing secure code and correct patches, have lagged behind . Also at the [un]prompted conference, OpenAI security researcher Tim de Waal showed how an AI agent patched two vulnerabilities in the firmware of a network access point. For one issue, the agent rebuilt the vulnerable function without the stack canaries the original code had, silently removing a defensive protection. For the other, the generated patch filtered out double-quote characters in the attacker input but missed that using single quotes would have bypassed the fix. Controlled studies found the same issue at scale. When researchers at 1Password’s Off-by-1 Labs used AI agents to repeatedly generate patches for the same six known vulnerabilities in complex open-source projects, about half of the 6,080 resulting patch candidates left at least one attack path open , with agents sometimes missing identical instances of the same bug in other parts of the code. More recently, in a benchmark test called P2Patch , researchers pitted two AI agents against each other: one wrote exploits for 101 real vulnerabilities, and the other patched the code until the exploits stopped working. Then the first agent attacked the patched programs again, looking for a different way to trigger the same flaw. In 41 of the 101 cases, it succeeded, sometimes multiple times for subsequent patches. Of course, human-written patches are not infallible either. Security firm Trail of Bits reviewed the fixes developers submitted for 2,265 vulnerabilities found during its consulting assessments over several years and one in eight failed to fully resolve the reported issues. In one case the company documented, a human maintainer and an AI agent working as part of the Patch the Planet initiative separately wrote patches for the same memory-safety bug in the freenginx web server, and both patches introduced the same crash during request cleanup. Organizations turn to AI patching because humans can’t keep up The issue is not that AI always writes worse patches than humans, although the failure rate of AI-written patches might be higher, but that the rate of vulnerability discovery is now so fast that humans alone can’t keep up. This is combined with the offensive capabilities of AI agents that enable attackers to analyze and reverse engineer patches at machine speed. Seven months after launching its Mythos-powered Glasswing vulnerability-hunting program , Anthropic’s public ledger counted 37,966 findings. Only 217 of the 7,349 flaws that were made public had been fixed, according to a recent analysis from vulnerability intelligence firm VulnCheck. Not all findings turn out to be security vulnerabilities, but Anthropic claims a true positive rate of 94.2%, which, given the small number of fixes, highlights the deluge of reports that maintainers have to triage and deal with. “Progress on software security used to be limited by how quickly we could find new vulnerabilities,” Anthropic wrote in its initial Glasswing update . “Now it’s limited by how quickly we can verify, disclose, and patch the large numbers of vulnerabilities found by AI.” And this is not just a problem for open-source projects. After Bank of America let Anthropic’s models loose on its own systems, the bank added 1,000 outside contractors in the second quarter of this year to help with the patching work, on top of the roughly 3,000 existing staff. They were still on the job in October, CEO Brian Moynihan told CNBC . By July, Meta was using AI to write fixes for 40% of its critical vulnerabilities, and almost half of those patches landed in production unchanged. Despite that, the exposure time did not go down, Meta software engineer David Molnar said in a separate presentation at [un]prompted. That’s because the AI-proposed patches still had to be reviewed by humans, while the amount of new code grew more than 100% year over year, with more than 80% of it attributed to AI coding agents. “Everyone is drowning in stuff to review,” Molnar said, adding that his team has worked with directors and product managers internally to find more places where automation can be introduced, including in the review process, shifting it from human-in-the-loop to human-on-the-loop . “You can automate everything upstream of AI, and then just completely overwhelm your poor humans on the other end,” he said. “Which is why you have to take a look at the entire pipeline and automate all of it.” In June, the Forum of Incident Response and Security Teams (FIRST) projected around 66,000 CVE assignments for this year. With two months left, the number is already approaching 100,000. Microsoft’s October Patch Tuesday alone addressed 1,415 vulnerabilities compared to only 180 in October 2025. Closed-source patches are not safe from AI analysis If AI agents are scouring code repositories for vulnerability variants, one might be inclined to think that closed-source sofware, where the patch is usually inside a compiled binary, are safer. That’s not necessarily the case given that AI models are now also great at reverse engineering, and some people use them to create open-source replicas of complex proprietary products, for example Adobe Photoshop . In June, when Anthropic’s researchers tested what an attacker can do with AI-assisted patch diffing , they gave a model nothing beyond what’s public on patch day. It produced a working exploit within an hour of a Firefox fix landing. On Windows, given vulnerable and patched binaries plus decompilation output, the same approach built eight full privilege-escalation chains from 21 kernel vulnerabilities for roughly $2,000 each. “In some ways, N-days are the more dangerous of the two [compared to zero-days], because the patch itself provides a roadmap to the bug,” the Anthropic researchers said at the time. A team of researchers from Fudan University in Shanghai, China, built an LLM-assisted binary diffing framework and analyzed 76 recent patches from 62 closed-source applications across 25 vendors. According to their paper published this month, the framework flagged 63 of the patches as incomplete and manually confirmed 56, of which 26 could be bypassed into new vulnerabilities, resulting in 19 CVE assignments and $28,100 in bug bounties. Comparing a vulnerable build against a patched one to locate the changed code has been a standard practice for security researchers for years. The difference now is the speed and lack of skill needed thanks to AI. And even though the latest frontier AI models might have API guardrails that make reverse engineering or binary diffing harder, the open-weight models have become capable enough. Taesoo Kim, vice president of security research at Microsoft, also warned during the [un]prompted conference that AI has drastically reduced the time needed for binary-diff analysis and exploit creation, and noted that Microsoft has to also be extremely careful when publishing CVEs and push updates quickly to customers. The more recent frontier models have started refusing such binary analysis work due to stricter guardrails, but a lot of people use open-weight models instead, such as Qwen, Kimi, and GLM, because “they are extremely capable,” he said. Exploiting the patch gap is now easy Last month, the Microsoft Edge Security team warned that attackers are increasingly taking advantage of the time gap between when information about a potential vulnerability becomes available in a code commit or test release in one project and when the patch trickles down to other projects. Their report included examples of attackers exploiting security fixes revealed in Chromium builds, the open-source browser that serves as the base for Google Chrome, Microsoft Edge, and other browsers, before those fixes were integrated in those downstream browsers. “This is patch-gap abuse,” the Edge team said . “The technique is not new, but the speed and expertise required is changing. AI-assisted analysis and exploit development could compress work that once took weeks into hours, increasing the chance that a usable exploit emerges while either exposure window remains open.” Researchers from Epoch AI recently used GLM 5.3 to emulate an unsophisticated attacker and target the Firefox patch gap. Using about $1,000 in API credits and as little as 12 hours of work per target, it compromised every Firefox release shipped between Sept. 17 and Oct. 26. “We did not trigger any safeguards or refusals from any provider,” the researchers wrote . In response, the Mozilla team has decided to take several actions to prevent patch gap abuse, for example by no longer releasing the regression tests associated with security fixes. “We’ve observed that GLM 5.3 is much less effective at patch-gapping when a regression test is not present, so we’ve reintroduced a practice of keeping these confidential until after the fix has shipped,” Firefox CTO Bobby Holley wrote . More diligence in patching, not less disclosure In a report last month dubbed PatchSlop, security firm Terra found that the rate of incomplete or broken fixes across open-source projects increased eightfold this year . “A patch that only blocks the reported input can give the impression the bug is addressed even if it’s still there in the underlying code,” the company’s researchers said. “It functions as a map for attackers, marking out both vulnerable code and what the defender thought the bug was. Looking just outside the diff (another encoding, another address range, another path into the same function) is one of the cheapest forms of bug hunting. We believe a growing share of attacker effort, and AI tokens, goes into exactly this.” The answer is not for open-source projects and software companies to hide vulnerability details and stop publishing security advisories, but to produce better patches. And some researchers believe this is possible, even when patching gets automated with the help of AI agents. In Rubrik’s case, after the company noticed that bugs it had marked as fixed kept coming back, Nejad’s team added its own variant hunting step that runs automatically in the pipeline after fixes are developed. The company began routing simple bugs to AI patching while reserving complex flaws, such as authentication bypasses, for human engineers. “Yes, attackers do have that context, but you have that context first, and you can act on that,” Nejad said. In a blog post this month , OpenAI noted that its Linux vulnerability research and patching pipeline needed iterative testing and variant analysis because initial patches “failed to examine related code for variants of the same vulnerability, leading to incomplete patches.” “We recommend using models for adversarial review of human and AI-generated patches, which can identify issues such as the patch being bypassable, missing other attack paths or variants, and more,” the company’s researchers said. The Open Source Security Foundation’s guidance for AI-assisted patching also advises teams to “have a new discovery agent probe the patch as an attacker” and Trail of Bits has released an agent skill that requires testing at least one distinct variant based on the bug’s root cause before a patch can be submitted. “It is clear there needs to be greater diligence and rigor when patching vulnerabilities,” Terra CEO Shahar Peled told CSO. “This means finding the root cause of any flaw, searching across the codebase for similar bugs and re-testing the system to ensure the patch itself doesn’t introduce a new vulnerability.”

title: Government science advisers: ‘No framework for datacentre demand’
raw_text:
The UK has no agreed method for working out how much onshore datacentre capacity it needs, and delays in securing grid connections are a key factor in where new sites go.

That’s according to the Government Office for Science, which published a report of a meeting chaired by chief scientific adviser Angela McLean in February. The report represents “the combined views of roundtable participants” and is explicitly “not a statement of government policy” but does provide useful insight into the datacentre debate at national planning level.

According to the report, the group found “no obvious frameworks to determine how much onshore datacentre capacity the UK will need in the future”, and said demand was “very hard to estimate”. Sizing decisions should start from what UK capacity is essential – where offshore provision is not an option, it said – and from tasks datacentres perform across the economy, rather than from sector-by-sector demand.

“Water is not a major constraint on datacentre siting in the UK,” it said. The notes state that datacentres can be cooled without water using closed-loop systems and ventilation, given the UK’s climate, and that Amazon Web Services’ facilities reportedly run waterless for around 97% of the year. It notes the trade-off is power, and using less water means using more electricity.

The roundtable recommended the UK build a national interactive map of every datacentre, plotting sites alongside fibre routes, power lines and other infrastructure. The aim is to give developers, planners and communities a shared picture of where capacity sits, from hyperscale campuses down to small edge sites.

The notes draw a line between workloads that need to stay in the UK and those that do not. Regulated public services and industries under data protection rules such as GDPR generally require onshore sites, it said, and there are “strong arguments” for onshore capacity to serve national security and defence. Ultra-low-latency tasks – high-frequency trading and growing financial artificial intelligence (AI) use among them – also tie capacity to specific locations.

Much of the rest can go elsewhere, says the report. The notes say many workloads tolerate some latency or are not sensitive to data location, so they can use offshore facilities or, in future, centralised mega datacentres. They cite Ukraine’s experience of hostile actors as a reason to favour offshore or distributed capacity for resilience.

Grid connections are cited as a pinch point. The notes say delays in establishing a grid connection are a key factor in siting and “risk undermining the UK’s digital growth objectives”. They float removing the government requirement for new power generation to be connected to the grid as a way to cut delays and improve national resilience.

Planning is another gap identified. There is currently no national planning guidance for datacentre siting, and the notes point to strategies in the Netherlands and Saudi Arabia as references. They argue clearer guidance would give developers and communities more certainty, and that public acceptance depends on people seeing a national need, clear local benefits and developers they trust.

The timing coincides with lively debate decisions on planning, grid connections and datacentre location. 

The debate nationally lacks reliable figures. Computer Weekly analysis published this week has highlighted the dearth of reliable data around datacentre planning, in particular with regard to electricity draw, water use, and even the numbers of datacentres in existence and in the pipeline.

Computer Weekly has spent several months attempting to build reliable estimates. It has drawn on the Barbour ABI construction database and Energy Performance Certificate registers and found 88 verified existing UK datacentre sites with a combined capacity of about 1.6GW, against a committed pipeline of 173 schemes and about 14.6GW. The recommendation for a national map echoes that work. The numbers are contested because no shared, verified inventory exists.

Demand uncertainty runs through the meeting notes. The roundtable said future capacity would be variable and geographic, would depend on balance between small firms and large consumers, and would hinge on the pace of AI adoption – which itself depends on domestic datacentre capacity. It acknowledged that over-provisioning may be necessary to absorb that uncertainty, and that AI and non-AI services are already blurring as cloud sites evolve into combined general and AI facilities.

It acknowledged that workloads differ sharply. Training AI models is generally less latency-sensitive than running them, and for some large language models, demand has shifted from training to inference, which the notes say carries a significantly greater environmental impact at scale. Image processing for agriculture and transport is among the fastest-growing uses and typically needs localised capacity because of the volume of data involved.

Nine people took part in the roundtable. Alongside Angela McLean, the roundtable included Clive Richardson (Amazon Web Services), Dawn Childs (Pure Data Centres Group), Dimitra Simeonidou (University of Bristol), Eve Schooler (University of Oxford), John Booth (BCS, The Chartered Institute for IT), Luisa Cardani (TechUK), Patrick Devine-Wright (Exeter University) and Tim Watson (Loughborough University).

No grid or energy system operator sat at the table, and no water or planning regulator, even though grid delays and planning are two of the report’s central themes. The notes also carry the caution that they are advice, not a decision. The government has not committed to the map, to planning guidance or to changing grid connection rules.

The eight-month gap between meeting and publication points to a slow clearance loop in a fast-moving area. In that time, the UK pressed ahead with AI growth zones and datacentre planning decisions against capacity and demand figures that, by the advisers’ own account, nobody has a framework to test.

Waste heat and climate add further constraints. The notes say reuse needs datacentres sited near infrastructure that can use the heat, and that opportunities are limited without district heat networks and when sites sit on former industrial or greenfield land. Possible use cases include laundry, food preparation and greenhouses. Siting must also adapt to flooding, temperature and water availability.

title: Data dive: The UK datacentre numbers that don’t add up
raw_text:
The UK datacentre debate seems to run on a handful of numbers. There are 520 of them, or 500, or 450. Meanwhile, they are in the queue for 73GW (gigawatts) or 57.88GW of grid connections, and that translates to 315 datacentres.

They drink 6.6 million litres of water a day, which will soon be 19.8 million, or 14 million, or 42 million, depending on which paper you read. Each figure is put out there with great confidence. Almost none of them survive contact with evidence.

The numbers travel through the documents that steer policy. This includes written evidence to the Environmental Audit Committee, Ofgem consultations, Freedom of Information responses from the National Energy System Operator (NESO), and submissions from the water industry. From there, they pass into the Guardian, the Times, the Daily Mail and the BBC. By the time a council, a minister or a resident cites them, the trail back to the original data is cold.

Computer Weekly has spent months building a more forensic picture of the same territory, using the Barbour ABI construction database and the Energy Performance Certificate (EPC) registers to count what exists, what is planned and what it might draw.

This article traces the headline numbers to their source, tests them against that research, and asks why approximations keep getting reported as fact. The answers matter because these figures appear in influential publications, serve as ammunition for campaign groups, and make their way into documents submitted to Parliament, where decisions on planning, water and grid capacity are made against them.

The 500-datacentre illusion

The most repeated figure is the simplest, and the shakiest. The UK government’s own investment website tells overseas investors that Britain “hosts over 520 datacentres, the largest market in Western Europe”. TechUK put the count at 500 in its 2025 water report. The Guardian used 520 and 450 within days of each other. The range, 450 to 520, has hardened into a “fact” of the datacentre debate.

Our analysis of non-domestic EPC registers – which show the certificates every large building must have – found 57,026 large non-domestic properties, of which 229 scored as datacentre candidates. After checking each against planning records, operator directories and press reports, 88 stand up as confirmed existing sites, with 20 campus duplicates. Their combined capacity is about 1.6GW.

Meanwhile, the 450 to 520 range appears to be a count of buildings on commercial directories, not of verified sites. Data Center Map, the directory these counts are usually drawn from, now lists just over 600 UK facilities – but a directory entry is not a working datacentre, and many are single buildings on multi-building campuses, planned rather than live sites, or duplicates.

The EPC method has limits. It is a lower bound. It misses buildings under about 2,000m2 and very new sites that have not yet been certified. But it is built on energy performance certificates, not marketing content. The distance between “over 520” and roughly 90 verified sites is the gap between a directory entry and an actual datacentre.

TL;DR – The datacentre numbers that don’t add up

  • The “520 datacentres” claim traces to a directory count; EPC-based counting confirms fewer than 100 substantial sites, roughly 1.6GW in total.
  • The 73GW and 315-project grid queue is a register of speculative positions, not a construction pipeline; committed capacity in planning is about 14.6GW.
  • Water UK’s 6.6 million litres-a-day figure rests on self-reported ranges from 73 sites, extrapolated to 500 – precision the underlying data cannot support.
  • Affinity Water’s “125 proposed datacentres” produced three actual planning applications.
  • The claim that datacentres use 2.5% of UK electricity, rising fourfold by 2030, rests on a committee chair’s framing; analysis of DESNZ data puts the 2024 share at 1.8%.

A queue, not a pipeline

While the datacentre count inflates what exists, the grid queue inflates what’s coming. Ofgem’s July consultation stated that “around 73GW across approximately 315 projects” of datacentre demand sits in the connection queue. The Guardian repeated those numbers, and upgraded them all to “hyperscale datacentres”. The figures read like a forecast, but they are not.

The first problem is provenance. The 73GW is not Ofgem’s invention – it is NESO’s own figure, rounded up. NESO’s written evidence to the Environmental Audit Committee states that “new pipeline data collected in 2025 from distribution and transmission network operators shows around 72.8GW of connection requests through to 2039”, which it says is “a huge step change in demand in the sector”.

Of that, nearly 59GW sits at transmission level (the high-voltage national grid) and the remainder on the regional distribution networks (lower-voltage local grids). NESO’s transmission figure is the part it will stand behind – 57.88GW in its FOI response.

Asked to account for the distribution portion, NESO told Computer Weekly: “As we don’t own the distribution data, we can’t verify these numbers.” So, the headline number rests partly on a distribution figure that the body which published it now says it cannot verify.

Ofgem’s press office went further. Its July 2026 press release that announced the reforms said demand connection applications “have surged from 41GW to 125GW, in under a year. This rise is driven largely by datacentre projects, accounting for at least 80GW”. Asked how those figures were reached, Ofgem told Computer Weekly they “were provided to Ofgem by NESO” – an 80GW figure NESO has never published, and 7GW above the 72.8GW total it did publish.

The second problem is how the data is characterised. Asked how the “nearly 59GW” was derived, NESO said in an FOI response that it holds a dataset of “transmission connected demand” with an “assigned technology type”, and that it “carried out internal analysis in order to identify what we believe to be the datacentres within this dataset. This is where the figure of 59GW has been calculated from”.

Some judgement is unavoidable – there is no official register, and our own count is an inference too – but the difference is in how it is disclosed. NESO published no method, no thresholds and no project-level breakdown until FOI requests drew them out. And the numbers change between its documents without stated reconciliation. Its parliamentary evidence, drawn from 2025 pipeline data, puts “nearly 59GW” at transmission level with “40 of the 173 projects” between 500MW and 1,500MW, while its October 2026 FOI response gives 57.88GW across 164 projects, 36 of them in that band.

The third problem is what we consider a queue actually amounts to. Connection applications are positions reserved by developers, not schemes with planning consent, finance or a customer. Our Barbour ABI analysis finds 173 projects, totalling about 14.6GW, that have entered the planning system and are not yet built. That is real money and real land, and it is barely a fifth of the 73GW headline, which looks more like a ledger of options that will never be exercised.

Water: Precision built on buckets

The water numbers carry a great deal of weight too, because they were also placed directly before Parliament. On 2 April 2026, Water UK told the Environmental Audit Committee that “datacentres currently use approximately 6.6 million litres of water per day”, rising to 19.8 million if the government’s plan to triple capacity by 2030 holds. The figures have since been repeated by the Guardian, the Times and the BBC, and by campaign groups keen to show the thirst of the datacentre build-out.

Footnote 16 of that submission explains the method. The figure, it says, is “Water UK analysis based on a sample size of 116 datacentres (almost a quarter of the estimated 500 datacentres in the UK – see TechUK (2025))”, and “was extrapolated out from the sample to estimate the whole sector’s usage”.

The “TechUK (2025)” report referred to can be read here, and the “500 datacentres” cited by Water UK is likely the upper figure of the “450 to 500” on page 9. Here, we are directed to a footnote that points towards a previous TechUK report that contains no reference to the number of datacentres in the UK.

When we asked how its figure was built, Water UK first said: “We didn’t use TechUK figures for datacentre water use.” It then explained that the estimate was “based on how much water the water companies supplied to datacentres from a sample, which was then extrapolated out to meet the number in the report – 500 datacentres”, but did not attribute a source. By its final email, the 500 was again “taken from the TechUK report”.

However you read that, any pretence at precision is unsupported. TechUK’s survey, run with the Environment Agency, drew 80 responses and 73 usable sites – not 116 – and it did not collect precise figures.

It said: “Sites that did [measure] were asked to select their average annual consumption from a set of ranges.” These buckets were “less than 1,000m³, 1,000-10,000m³, 10,001-100,000m³, and more than 100,000m³”. It added: “We collected annual consumption in ranges rather than exact figures.” No totals were produced.

Those ranges are enormous. The two middle buckets each span a factor of 10. The top bucket has no ceiling. A site logged as “more than 100,000m³” could be 100,000 or 2,000,000. And because water use is intensely skewed – the MOSL/WRc study found six sites accounted for 65% of the sector’s consumption – the national total is really a statement about a handful of buildings in the widest, open-ended range. To reach a precise 6.6 million litres a day, someone has to assume where each site sits. Water UK has not published those assumptions.

The metered market tells a calmer story. MOSL, which runs England’s non-household water market, estimates datacentres use about 1.9 billion litres a year, or roughly 0.2% of non-household consumption. Water companies lose about three billion litres a day to leaks.

The gap between projection and reality is stark elsewhere too, and adds to the evidence against unverified queue figures.

Affinity Water, which serves a region that includes datacentre hotspot Slough, told MPs that “approximately 125 datacentres are either proposed or under construction” in its area. That figure came from planning database Glenigans, it said, but we have no idea how the data was filtered. When Affinity tracked which of those 125 reached the planning process, the answer was three.

“Only three have come through to actual proposals, or actual planning applications,” its public affairs adviser, Richard Emmott, told Computer Weekly.

The Guardian ran with the 125 figure. Meanwhile, the Affinity submission to Parliament also talked of “some individual facilities requesting supplies of up to 35 litres per second, equivalent to the peak water demand of 3,500 homes.” The Daily Mail and Huffington Post ran with that figure.

Affinity Water’s Emmott told Computer Weekly that the 35 litres per second request was a peak demand projection for firefighting purposes. He also said the datacentre demand Affinity can verify is “less than one megalitre per day”, which contrasts with 950 megalitres of daily supply.

Computer Weekly has already shown how a single misread figure can distort the water debate. In that case, a report by the Government Digital Sustainability Alliance (GDSA) looked in detail at water consumption associated with artificial intelligence (AI) and datacentres, and made an established fact of a “five billion litres a day” shortfall by 2050 when it is actually the worst-case scenario in the Environment Agency’s planning. The best case – assuming infrastructure improvements – shows a surplus.

These numbers come in many cases from submissions to Parliament. A trade body that puts a precise figure to a select committee should be held to it. There is public interest in reporting the kind of discrepancies we find here, because of the effect they can have on datacentre planning and public opinion.

Electricity draw: What we know, what we don’t

The figures cited for datacentre electricity use also come with some uncertainty. In a 16 April 2026 notice launching a Science, Innovation and Technology Committee inquiry, its chair, Dame Chi Onwurah, wrote that “datacentres currently use about 2.5% of the UK’s electricity, but their consumption is expected to rise fourfold by 2030”. It was a framing remark at an inquiry launch into an uncertain question, not a finding.

Measured against our research on datacentre electricity, the 2.5% figure overstates, and the projected rise is just that – a projection with no apparent calculation we can examine. Our analysis of Department for Energy Security and Net Zero (DESNZ) data finds UK datacentres used 1.8% of Great Britain’s grid electricity in 2024, up from 1.2% in 2020 – the most recent published breakdown that separates datacentres out.

That is now two years old, and the estate has grown since, so today’s true share will be higher. The open question is, how much higher? The fourfold projection to 10% by 2030 is where the trouble lies – a committed pipeline of roughly nine times the existing estate makes the direction plausible, but the specific figure rests on a capacity trajectory with no published details.

Why the numbers inflate

Each distortion in the numbers has a beneficiary.

The circa 500 datacentre count serves companies that sell property and investment intelligence, as well as trade bodies that benefit from appearing to be at the centre of a boom.

The grid queue numbers are populated by a place in line that is currently a cheap option for a developer – easy to hold, easy to abandon – and all calculated to help attract investment. For Ofgem, NESO and the network operators, the worst-case figure such activities generate is a lever that helps justify commitment fees and queue reforms, and strengthens the case for investment in the network.

Water use estimates serve an industry under pressure to justify investment, and campaign groups for whom a bigger number drives urgency.

Journalists, who use what are essentially lobby-supplied figures, can only presume an editorial line driven by politics. But the result is to undermine the scrutiny journalists exist to apply. When an ostensibly progressive paper repeats a trade body’s estimate as fact, the number acquires a weight in Westminster that its data never earned.

How we built our numbers

Our figures on the existing datacentre estate and those in the planning process come from two datasets, and both carry limits we state openly. The existing estate is inferred from non-domestic EPC registers. Of 57,026 large non-domestic buildings, 229 scored as datacentre candidates, and 88 survived manual verification. Capacity is published in megawatts where a site discloses it, but otherwise modelled from floor area – around 1,166W per square metre for colocation and 800W for enterprise. It is an estimated lower bound, not a metered load.

The pipeline is drawn from data from Barbour ABI, a construction planning tracking service. We count as “active” only projects that have entered the planning system and are not yet built. The most recent count made 173 schemes, and about 14.6GW. Capacity is taken from the project text where stated, modelled from floor area where not, estimated from trade and press reports in a few cases, while 28 schemes carry no megawatt figure and are excluded from the capacity total. We do not count “pre-planning” announcements as part of the pipeline.

These methods are imperfect. What sets them apart from the public numbers is that they are published, reproducible and open to challenge.

Reliable planning needs reliable numbers

The datacentre build-out is real, and its demands on water and power are serious enough to justify hard questions. But the debate has settled on a set of numbers that are often quite unreliable – a datacentre marketing directory presented as built reality, a queue of options presented as a committed pipeline, self-reported ranges presented as a precise national figure, and a committee chair’s aside presented as a finding. Each flatters the case of whoever is citing it, but almost all collapse when traced to their source.

Until someone publishes a datacentre demand forecast with a stated baseline, a transparent method and a confidence range, the planning, water and grid decisions now being taken will rest on numbers that cannot bear their weight. Britain may well need datacentres, but it cannot afford to build them on figures it can’t defend.
